summary:
No measure, incident, arrest, ban or institution concerning trans visitors is recorded in Sinop itself in the audited sources. What a trans visitor to Sinop faces is the Turkish national framework, and no Sinop authority is documented adding enforcement or prohibitions of its own.

Sinop stands under the national framework of Turkey. Homosexuality was decriminalised in 1858 under the Ottoman penal code and legal gender change has been possible since 1988, but same-sex marriage is not recognised and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military. Pride events have been repeatedly blocked by governors: the 2015 to 2018 Istanbul parades were banned by local authorities, and on 14 June 2019 the Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya prides were all banned by the cities' governors. A proposal to criminalise publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex' with a one-to-three-year prison sentence was ultimately not included in the 12th judicial package.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records that in June 2025 blanket bans were issued against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. Three draft law packages made public in 2025 would criminalise LGBTI identity expression and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible; none was submitted to parliament.
tangentialFactors:
The bans and prosecutions Amnesty documents concern Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya, not Sinop; they evidence the national posture a visitor to Sinop still stands under, but no Sinop-specific enforcement is recorded.

The draft packages criminalising LGBTI identity expression and consensual same-sex relations, and the proposal on 'behavior contrary to biological sex' that was dropped from the 12th judicial package, remain unresolved as to current status in the sources.
localsOnly:
For Sinop residents, the practical exposure is the national framework: legal gender change has been available since 1988, but same-sex marriage is unrecognised, open service in the military is barred, and the draft packages under consideration would make legal gender recognition nearly impossible.

Local pride organising anywhere in Turkey, including Sinop, sits under a pattern of gubernatorial bans; the 2019 simultaneous bans in Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya show the power governors exercise over such events.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any of the three 2025 draft law packages has since been submitted to parliament is unresolved in the sources.

No source in this inventory documents any Sinop-specific authority, incident, ban or enforcement measure concerning trans visitors; the assessment rests on the national layer alone.
